title: Query Performance
intro: A query that is fast with a few hundred records can become a serious bottleneck with several million records. In this lesson, you will learn how indexes help, how to read an SQL execution plan, and how to design effective pagination.
body:
## Why do queries become slow?

When an application starts out, it often works with only a small amount of data.

You might have 50 users and 500 tasks. A simple query will run almost instantly.

~~~sql
SELECT *
FROM tasks
WHERE user_id = 3;
~~~

With a few thousand records, you probably still won't notice any problems.

But imagine the same thing with 20 million tasks.

If the database has to inspect every record for every query, the amount of work increases along with the amount of data.

That is why it is important to understand that an SQL query is not only about whether it returns the correct result. It is also important **how the database gets to that result**.

This is what we call query performance.

Performance can be affected by several things:

- the amount of data,
- the structure of the query,
- indexes,
- JOINs,
- sorting,
- the amount of data returned,
- the pagination method,
- database resources,
- and the connection pool used by the application.

---

## What is an index?

The easiest way to think about an index is as the index of a book.

~~~widget index-scan
~~~

If you want to find every page in a 1000-page book where a particular concept appears, you don't want to read through the entire book.

The index helps you quickly find the relevant pages.

A database index serves a similar purpose.

Suppose you frequently run:

~~~sql
SELECT id, title
FROM tasks
WHERE user_id = 3;
~~~

A `user_id` index can help the database find the matching records more quickly.

In PostgreSQL, one of the most common index types is **B-tree**.

You do not need to know the complete implementation of the data structure right now. The important point is that an index provides an ordered structure that allows the database to inspect far fewer records when searching.

Think of it roughly like this:

~~~text
             50
           /    \
         25      75
        /  \    /  \
      10   40  60   90
~~~

Instead of checking every value one by one, the database can use the index structure to find the relevant search range more quickly.

### Indexes have a cost

An index is not free, however.

If you create an index:

~~~sql
CREATE INDEX idx_tasks_user_id
ON tasks(user_id);
~~~

then the database also has to maintain the index.

This means that `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, and in some cases `DELETE` operations can become more expensive.

An index also takes up storage space.

That is why the goal is not to create an index on every column.

**A good index is one that speeds up a genuinely important query, and whose benefit is greater than its maintenance cost.**

---

## Which columns should you index?

Indexes can be particularly useful on columns that you frequently use in:

- `WHERE` conditions,
- `JOIN` conditions,
- `ORDER BY` clauses,
- and in some cases `GROUP BY` operations.

For example:

~~~sql
SELECT *
FROM tasks
WHERE user_id = 42;
~~~

Here, a `user_id` index may be useful.

For a JOIN:

~~~sql
SELECT t.title, u.name
FROM tasks t
JOIN users u ON u.id = t.user_id;
~~~

Properly indexing the columns used for relationships can be important, especially for large tables.

For sorting:

~~~sql
SELECT id, title
FROM tasks
WHERE user_id = 42
ORDER BY created_at DESC;
~~~

Here, a properly designed index can help with both filtering and sorting.

But you should not simply guess which index is the right choice. Look at the actual query plan.

---

## Composite indexes

You do not always create an index on a single column.

For example, suppose you frequently run:

~~~sql
SELECT id, title
FROM tasks
WHERE user_id = 3
  AND status = 'open';
~~~

You can create a composite index for this:

~~~sql
CREATE INDEX idx_tasks_user_status
ON tasks(user_id, status);
~~~

This is a single index containing two columns.

The order of the columns is very important.

~~~text
(user_id, status)
~~~

is not the same as:

~~~text
(status, user_id)
~~~

How useful the index is depends on the conditions you search with.

If you frequently filter by `user_id` and then by `status`, the `(user_id, status)` index may be a good fit.

If, however, you do not use the first column of an index at all in the query, the database may not be able to take advantage of the index in the same way.

That is why the actual query pattern should always be the starting point when designing a composite index.

---

## EXPLAIN: see what the database plans to do

One of PostgreSQL's most important performance diagnostic tools is `EXPLAIN`.

~~~compare
{"left": {"title": "Without index", "lang": "text", "code": "Seq Scan on users\n  Filter: (email = 'oliver@mail.hu')\n  Rows Removed by Filter: 999999\n  Execution Time: 182.4 ms", "note": "Every row was read and thrown away."}, "right": {"title": "With index", "lang": "text", "code": "Index Scan using users_email_idx\n  Index Cond: (email = 'oliver@mail.hu')\n  Execution Time: 0.06 ms", "note": "The plan names the index — that is your proof."}}
~~~

For example:

~~~sql
EXPLAIN
SELECT *
FROM tasks
WHERE user_id = 3
  AND status = 'open';
~~~

`EXPLAIN` shows you which execution plan PostgreSQL has chosen.

We do not only want to know whether the query is correct. We also want to see how the database plans to execute it.

### Seq Scan

A common plan is `Seq Scan`, meaning sequential scan.

Simply put, this means that the database can read through the table's records sequentially and select the ones that match the condition.

This can be completely fine for a small table.

However, if you have tens of millions of records and are looking for only a few records, scanning the entire table can be expensive.

### Index Scan

If a suitable index exists, PostgreSQL may decide to find the required records using an `Index Scan`.

For example, with a suitable index:

~~~text
Index Scan using idx_tasks_user_status on tasks
~~~

This indicates that the query planner chose to use an index.

However, it is important to understand that **an Index Scan is not always better**.

If the query wants to return a very large portion of the table's records, a sequential scan can actually be more efficient.

The database query planner makes its choice based on cost estimates.

---

## EXPLAIN ANALYZE

`EXPLAIN` shows you a plan.

`EXPLAIN ANALYZE`, on the other hand, actually executes the query and also shows you the real runtime information.

~~~sql
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT id, title
FROM tasks
WHERE user_id = 3
  AND status = 'open';
~~~

This is particularly useful when investigating performance problems.

In the result, you may encounter estimated and actual row counts, as well as cost information.

The important idea is that you can compare the plan chosen by the database with what actually happened during execution.

**Measure before you optimize.**

---

## Only query what you need

A common beginner mistake is:

~~~sql
SELECT *
FROM tasks
WHERE user_id = 3;
~~~

If the frontend actually only needs the ID and title, this is better:

~~~sql
SELECT id, title
FROM tasks
WHERE user_id = 3;
~~~

This has several advantages.

You read less data from the database, send less data over the network, and the application also has less data to process.

This is especially important for wide tables where a record contains many large fields.

The same principle is important with JPA. Do not load an entire entity whenever you actually only need two fields.

With a DTO projection, interface projection, or targeted query, you can retrieve only the data you need.

---

## Pagination: LIMIT and OFFSET

If an API contains thousands of records, you do not want to send all of them at once.

Instead, we use pagination.

The classic approach is:

~~~sql
SELECT id, title
FROM tasks
ORDER BY id
LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40;
~~~

This can, for example, return something similar to the third page.

The problem appears with large offsets.

If you request:

~~~sql
LIMIT 20 OFFSET 1000000;
~~~

The database still has to deal with which records are in the first million positions before it reaches the page you actually want.

This can be expensive with very large datasets.

---

## Keyset pagination

**Keyset pagination**, also known as seek pagination, uses the previous position as its starting point.

~~~compare
{"left": {"title": "OFFSET pagination", "lang": "sql", "code": "SELECT * FROM task\nORDER BY id\nLIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000;", "note": "Reads and skips 100 000 rows first — slower on every page."}, "right": {"title": "Keyset pagination", "lang": "sql", "code": "SELECT * FROM task\nWHERE id > :lastSeenId\nORDER BY id\nLIMIT 20;", "note": "Jumps straight to the spot through the index."}}
~~~

Suppose you sort by ID and the last record on the previous page had an ID of `40`.

The next page is:

~~~sql
SELECT id, title
FROM tasks
WHERE id > 40
ORDER BY id
LIMIT 5;
~~~

This does not tell the database to "skip 40 records".

It says:

> Return the records that come after the most recently known position.

If `id` is properly indexed, this can be very efficient.

Keyset pagination is particularly useful for large tables and continuously increasing IDs.

### OFFSET or keyset?

Both have their place.

`OFFSET` is simple and convenient, for example on smaller administration pages.

Keyset pagination can be a better choice when you need to handle a large dataset, a stable sort order, and many pages.

---

## N+1 and JPA

Query performance problems do not only come directly from SQL.

When using JPA, the application code itself can also generate too many queries.

For example:

~~~java
List<Task> tasks = taskRepository.findAll();

for (Task task : tasks) {
    System.out.println(task.getUser().getName());
}
~~~

After loading the `Task` records, each individual User can trigger a separate query.

~~~text
1 query: tasks
+
N queries: users
=
N+1 queries
~~~

If you have 500 tasks, this can mean as many as 501 database queries.

One way to solve this is the `JOIN FETCH` we saw in the previous lesson:

~~~java
@Query("""
    SELECT t
    FROM Task t
    JOIN FETCH t.user
    WHERE t.done = false
""")
List<Task> findOpenTasksWithUser();
~~~

You can also use an `@EntityGraph` solution.

The key point is the same: **know how many database queries happen behind a single API request.**

---

## Connection pooling and HikariCP

A Spring Boot application should not create a new database connection for every SQL query. A connection pool maintains pre-created and reusable connections. In Spring Boot, HikariCP is the default connection pool for JDBC-based database connections. The application requests a connection from the pool, uses it, and then returns it. This avoids the repeated cost of creating and closing connections. However, you should not increase the pool size randomly: too many concurrent connections can put additional load on PostgreSQL itself.

---

## Measure before you optimize

One of the most important performance optimization rules is:

**Do not assume you know what is slow. Measure it.**

A query may appear slow because of Java code, but the majority of the work may actually be happening in the database.

A good process is:

~~~text
1. Measure the problem
       ↓
2. Look at the SQL
       ↓
3. EXPLAIN / EXPLAIN ANALYZE
       ↓
4. Identify the bottleneck
       ↓
5. Make a change
       ↓
6. Measure again
~~~

If a query runs in 5 ms, there may be no reason to create a complex optimization for it.

If the same query takes 3 seconds in a frequently used API endpoint, it is worth investigating the cause.

The goal of optimization is not to make every query as fast as possible, but to solve real performance problems.

---

## A practical example

Suppose your task manager uses this endpoint:

~~~text
GET /api/users/3/tasks?status=open
~~~

The query is:

~~~sql
SELECT id, title
FROM tasks
WHERE user_id = 3
  AND status = 'open'
ORDER BY id;
~~~

As the application's data grows, it is worth investigating this.

First, you look at the `EXPLAIN` plan.

If the query uses a sequential scan on a large table, you can investigate creating a composite index:

~~~sql
CREATE INDEX idx_tasks_user_status
ON tasks(user_id, status);
~~~

If you also use pagination, you can extend the query with keyset pagination:

~~~sql
SELECT id, title
FROM tasks
WHERE user_id = 3
  AND status = 'open'
  AND id > 40
ORDER BY id
LIMIT 5;
~~~

This is now a query whose performance can scale much better as the amount of data grows.

But again: you do not create the index because "every WHERE column needs an index". You design the index based on the actual workload and measured query performance.

---

## Common mistakes

### Indexing everything

More indexes do not automatically mean better performance. Every index takes up space and adds maintenance cost during writes.

### Using `SELECT *` everywhere

If you only need a few fields, retrieve only those fields. This can reduce the load on the database and network.

### Using large OFFSET values

For small datasets, `OFFSET` can be perfectly appropriate. With very large offsets, however, it is worth investigating keyset pagination.

### Creating indexes without measuring

An index can be useful, but it can also be completely unnecessary. First look at the query and the execution plan.

### Ignoring N+1

With JPA, a few lines of Java code can generate hundreds of SQL queries. Pay attention to both the generated SQL and the number of database calls.

### Automatically questioning the query planner's decision

If PostgreSQL chooses a `Seq Scan`, that is not necessarily a problem. On a small table or when returning many records, a sequential scan can be the appropriate strategy.

---

## Summary

Query performance is not about a single trick. Database performance is determined by the combination of queries, indexes, data volume, pagination, relationships, and the SQL generated by the application.

Indexes can speed up searches, but they come with write and storage costs. With composite indexes, the order of the columns matters. With `EXPLAIN`, you can see how PostgreSQL plans to execute a query, while `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` also shows actual runtime information.

With large datasets, keyset pagination can often scale better than using large `OFFSET` values. With JPA, always pay attention to the N+1 problem as well.

The most important rule remains simple: **measure, identify the real problem, make a change, then measure again.**
takeaways: Indexes can speed up WHERE, JOIN, and ORDER BY operations, but they require storage and add write overhead.
With composite indexes, the order of the columns matters, so design the index based on the actual query pattern.
PostgreSQL's EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE help you understand how a query is executed.
With large datasets, keyset pagination can be more efficient than using large OFFSET values.
Always optimize performance based on measurements, and pay particular attention to N+1 queries when using JPA.

quiz.question: What is one of the most important benefits of an index?
options: It makes every INSERT operation faster
It can help the database find the requested data while examining fewer records
It automatically normalizes the database
It prevents all SQL errors
quiz.explanation: With a suitable query, an index can allow the database to avoid scanning the entire table.

quiz.question: Why does the order of the columns in a `(user_id, status)` composite index matter?
options: Because the index only stores the first column
Because the database always sorts indexes alphabetically
Because how effectively the index can be used depends on how the query uses the columns on the left side of the index
Because PostgreSQL automatically deletes the second column
quiz.explanation: The structure of a composite index and the conditions in the query together determine how effectively the planner can take advantage of the index.

quiz.question: What does a `Seq Scan` mean in a PostgreSQL execution plan, in simple terms?
options: The database can read through the table's records sequentially
The database uses only an index
The query is definitely incorrect
PostgreSQL deletes and rebuilds the table
quiz.explanation: During a sequential scan, PostgreSQL examines the table's records sequentially. This is not necessarily a bad choice; for example, it can be appropriate for a small table.

quiz.question: Which query uses keyset pagination if the last ID on the previous page was 40?
options: SELECT * FROM tasks LIMIT 5 OFFSET 40;
SELECT * FROM tasks WHERE id < 40 ORDER BY id LIMIT 5;
SELECT * FROM tasks WHERE id > 40 ORDER BY id LIMIT 5;
SELECT * FROM tasks OFFSET 5 LIMIT 40;
quiz.explanation: With ascending ID-based pagination, the next page looks for records that come after the most recently known ID.

quiz.question: Why can using a large OFFSET value be problematic?
options: Because OFFSET always deletes data
Because the database has to process a large number of earlier records before reaching the requested page
Because OFFSET only works in PostgreSQL
Because OFFSET automatically generates an N+1 query
quiz.explanation: With a large offset, the database has to process or skip a significant number of earlier rows, which can be expensive on large tables.

exercise.title: Index and keyset pagination
exercise.task: In this exercise, you are working with a 200-row tasks table. First, create a composite index named `idx_tasks_user_status` using exactly the `(user_id, status)` columns. Then write a keyset pagination query that returns the next 5 tasks matching `user_id = 3` and `status = 'open'` where `id > 40`. The query should return only the `id` and `title` columns and sort by `id` in ascending order. The tests check the index name and columns, whether the SQLite EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN result uses the index, and whether the pagination returns exactly the expected next five records. Note: SQLite's EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN output is different from PostgreSQL's. In PostgreSQL, you would investigate the same problem using `EXPLAIN` or `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`.
exercise.setup:
PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;

CREATE TABLE tasks (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
  status TEXT NOT NULL,
  created_at TEXT NOT NULL,
  title TEXT NOT NULL
);

WITH RECURSIVE numbers(n) AS (
  SELECT 1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT n + 1 FROM numbers WHERE n < 200
)
INSERT INTO tasks (id, user_id, status, created_at, title)
SELECT
  n,
  ((n - 1) % 5) + 1,
  CASE
    WHEN n % 3 = 0 THEN 'done'
    ELSE 'open'
  END,
  printf('2026-01-%02dT%02d:00:00', ((n - 1) % 28) + 1, ((n - 1) % 24)),
  'Task ' || n
FROM numbers;
exercise.starter:
CREATE INDEX idx_tasks_user_status
ON tasks(user_id);

SELECT id, title
FROM tasks
WHERE user_id = 3
  AND status = 'open'
  AND id > 40
ORDER BY id
LIMIT 5;
exercise.solution:
CREATE INDEX idx_tasks_user_status
ON tasks(user_id, status);

SELECT id, title
FROM tasks
WHERE user_id = 3
  AND status = 'open'
  AND id > 40
ORDER BY id
LIMIT 5;
exercise.hint: The index should have exactly two columns, in this order: `user_id`, then `status`. For keyset pagination, you do not need OFFSET; instead, filter for records with an ID greater than the last ID on the previous page. At the end of the query, sort by `id` and request 5 records.

tests.name: The index is built on exactly the correct columns
The appropriate index is used by the SQLite query planner
Keyset pagination returns the correct next five tasks
